Do not give a dose.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"LactMed reports the following for **amoxicillin**:\\n\\n**Observed infant symptoms**\\n- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 mothers reported diarrhea in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)\\n- In a prospective study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breast milk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)\\n- In a study comparing amoxicillin with a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions among amoxicillin-exposed infants occurred in 8.3% and included rash and somnolence. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)\\n- A case report described a 2-month-old who developed generalized urticaria about 20 minutes after breastfeeding following the mother\u2019s first exposure to a combination of amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin. The hives recurred after a later breastfeeding episode. The report attributed the reaction probably to antibiotics in breast milk, but the responsible drug could not be determined; amoxicillin/clavulanate was considered most likely. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)\\n- Another report described mild diarrhea in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin and acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)\\n- In a study of 25 mothers whose infants were older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)\\n\\n**Advice to monitor**\\n- LactMed describes a study in which mothers were asked to monitor for tongue coating, feeding difficulties, changes in stool frequency or consistency, diaper rash, and skin rash; weight and jaundice were also recorded. These were study-assessment items, not evidence that those symptoms occurred or a separate general monitoring recommendation. [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)\\n- The retrieved LactMed text does not provide a distinct general recommendation to monitor for diarrhea, rash, thrush, or somnolence.\\n\\n**Measured exposure**\\n- Reported milk concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours, with a range of **0.46\u20130.88 mg/L**, and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours, with a range of **0.39\u20131.3 mg/L**. These are measured milk concentrations, not infant doses. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)\\n- For **infant levels**, LactMed states: \u201cRelevant published information was not found\u201d as of the revision date. The specimen type is therefore not available in the retrieved record. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n\\n**Uncertainty**\\n- LactMed states that rash and gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea or thrush have been reported but have not been adequately evaluated. The reports include small studies, parent reports, a combination-product exposure, and co-exposure to other medicines; the extract does not establish how often the symptoms occur or prove that amoxicillin alone caused each event. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n- The retrieved record was revised June 15, 2026. It is a bounded extract rather than an exhaustive record; missing or unreported findings do not establish safety or absence of effects. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)\\n- The MCP notes that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and that changes should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.\\n\\nApplication limits:\\nThis LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.\\nHuman clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.\\nStopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.\\n\\nInformational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. request.question: What does LactMed report about amoxicillin in breastfed babies? Separate observed symptoms from advice to monitor, and explain uncertainty. Do not give a dose.

response.answer:
LactMed reports the following for **amoxicillin**:

**Observed infant symptoms**
- In a telephone follow-up of 25 nursing mothers, 3 mothers reported diarrhea in their infants; no rash or candidiasis was reported in that study. [S10](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8498418/)
- In a prospective study of 40 infants exposed to amoxicillin in breast milk, 2 developed diarrhea and 1 developed a rash. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/16044108/)
- In a study comparing amoxicillin with a macrolide antibiotic, reported reactions among amoxicillin-exposed infants occurred in 8.3% and included rash and somnolence. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/19366316/)
- A case report described a 2-month-old who developed generalized urticaria about 20 minutes after breastfeeding following the mother’s first exposure to a combination of amoxicillin/clavulanate and gentamicin. The hives recurred after a later breastfeeding episode. The report attributed the reaction probably to antibiotics in breast milk, but the responsible drug could not be determined; amoxicillin/clavulanate was considered most likely. [S2](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1472-8206.2009.00689.x)
- Another report described mild diarrhea in an 11-month-old whose mother was taking amoxicillin and acetaminophen plus codeine; the relationship was rated possible or probable. [S7](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/40183105/)
- In a study of 25 mothers whose infants were older than 4 weeks, no infant adverse effects were reported. [S8](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/41582095/)

**Advice to monitor**
- LactMed describes a study in which mothers were asked to monitor for tongue coating, feeding difficulties, changes in stool frequency or consistency, diaper rash, and skin rash; weight and jaundice were also recorded. These were study-assessment items, not evidence that those symptoms occurred or a separate general monitoring recommendation. [S1](https://doi.org/10.1111/j.1365-2125.1991.tb05523.x)
- The retrieved LactMed text does not provide a distinct general recommendation to monitor for diarrhea, rash, thrush, or somnolence.

**Measured exposure**
- Reported milk concentrations were **0.69 mg/L** at 4 hours, with a range of **0.46–0.88 mg/L**, and **0.81 mg/L** at 5 hours, with a range of **0.39–1.3 mg/L**. These are measured milk concentrations, not infant doses. [S9](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/7246123/)
- For **infant levels**, LactMed states: “Relevant published information was not found” as of the revision date. The specimen type is therefore not available in the retrieved record. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)

**Uncertainty**
- LactMed states that rash and gastrointestinal effects such as diarrhea or thrush have been reported but have not been adequately evaluated. The reports include small studies, parent reports, a combination-product exposure, and co-exposure to other medicines; the extract does not establish how often the symptoms occur or prove that amoxicillin alone caused each event. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)
- The retrieved record was revised June 15, 2026. It is a bounded extract rather than an exhaustive record; missing or unreported findings do not establish safety or absence of effects. [S13](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK500887/)
- The MCP notes that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and that changes should be discussed with the prescribing clinician.

This LactMed response is a bounded extract, not a complete record. Omitted sections or truncation can limit the summary; absence of retrieved findings is not evidence of safety.

request.question: For sumatriptan during breastfeeding, what was measured in milk and what was actually observed in infants? If those are different kinds of evidence, explain that. No personal medication advice.

response.answer:
### Measured exposure

LactMed reports these **sumatriptan concentrations in breast milk**:

- Peak milk concentration: **87.2 mcg/L** (range **62–113 mcg/L**), measured in five breastfeeding women; sampling context was approximately **2.5 hours** after administration. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/8866921/)
- In a separate group of seven breastfeeding women, peak milk concentration averaged **59.3 mcg/L** (range **24.6–112.8 mcg/L**), occurring **2–4 hours** after administration. The average milk concentration was **23.2 mcg/L** (range **7.7–50.6 mcg/L**). [S2](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33730376/)

**Infant-level measurements:** LactMed states that relevant published information on infant levels was **not found as of the record’s revision date**. The retrieved information therefore concerns milk concentrations, not measured infant concentrations. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports manufacturer correspondence stating that, among **three women** known to the manufacturer who used sumatriptan while breastfeeding, **none reported adverse effects in their infants**. The exposure amount and route were unspecified. [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501255/)

These are different evidence types: milk concentrations measure **drug exposure in milk**; the three-person report describes **reported infant observations**. The milk measurements do not themselves establish an infant outcome, and the reported infant observations do not provide measured infant drug levels. The retrieved extract does not establish a study count and is not a safety verdict.

Application limits:

request.question: Is there an FDA-listed pregnancy exposure registry covering topiramate? Give the listing and registry contact or enrollment link if returned, and distinguish finding a registry from being eligible to enroll.

response.answer:
Yes. The FDA directory lists **The North American Antiepileptic Drug in Pregnancy Registry** for **Topamax, Trokendi XR, and Qudexy XR (topiramate)**, with **epilepsy, mood disorder, and migraine headaches** listed as conditions. Its status is **“Ongoing.”** [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

**Registry contact/enrollment link:** [https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)  
**Telephone:** Massachusetts General Hospital for Children, toll-free **1-888-233-2334**. [S1](https://www.aedpregnancyregistry.org/join-our-study/)

This confirms that a registry is listed; it does **not** establish that any particular person is eligible to enroll. Eligibility and current enrollment must be confirmed directly with the registry. FDA’s listing also states that it does not operate or endorse the registries and that its list is not comprehensive. [S2](https://www.fda.gov/consumers/pregnancy-exposure-registries/list-pregnancy-exposure-registries)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

response.answer:
## Recruiting U.S. ADHD studies involving children

The search returned two potential matches. The registry lists each source population as **“not established”**; the records include numeric child age ranges. These listings do not determine eligibility or recommend participation. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=ADHD+AND+%28child%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=United+States)

### 1. Digital Health Intervention for Children With ADHD — NCT06456372
- **Exact study link:** [S3](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06456372)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Source population:** Not established in the returned record
- **Overall status:** **RECRUITING**
- **Last update posted:** 2026-01-28
- **Age range listed:** 8–12 years; sex: all; healthy volunteers: no
- **Site status:**  
  - The Craig School, Irvine, California — **RECRUITING**  
  - UCR Psychiatry at Grindstaff Community School, Riverside, California — **RECRUITING**
- **Qualification limits listed:**  
  - DSM-5-TR ADHD diagnosis documented through prior medical or psychological evaluations  
  - Ability to complete questionnaires and use an app in English  
  - Reported IQ of at least 80  
  - Parent/guardian available to consent and provide feedback in English
- **Contacts:**  
  - Jaime Smith — 951-827-0741; jaime.smith@medsch.ucr.edu  
  - Kimberley Lakes — 951-827-2410; kimberley.lakes@medsch.ucr.edu  
  - Site contact: Nancy Herrera, PhD — nancy.herrera@medsch.ucr.edu

### 2. Enhancing Team Effectiveness for a Collaborative School-based Intervention for ADHD — NCT06180681
- **Exact study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT06180681)
- **Study type:** Interventional
- **Source population:** Not established in the returned record
- **Overall status:** **RECRUITING**
- **Last update posted:** 2026-06-30
- **Age range listed:** 7–11 years; sex: all; healthy volunteers: no
- **Site status:**  
  - IN STEP Children’s Mental Health Center, San Diego, California — **RECRUITING**
- **Qualification limits listed:**  
  - Ages 7–11 and attending a participating school  
  - Referral by a school mental-health provider for apparent ADHD-related problems  
  - At least 6 specified inattention or hyperactivity/impulsivity symptoms and impairment ratings meeting the registry criteria  
  - Caregiver and teacher consent; child assent  
  - Exclusions listed include certain severe impairments or conditions, attendance in an all-day special-education classroom, inability of the child or caregiver to read or speak English or Spanish, and planned changes to psychotropic medication  
  - The record states that children taking attention or behavior medication must have stable regimens
- **Contact:**  
  - Lilliana Conradi, BA — 16196513154; lconradi@health.ucsd.edu

request.question: Are any recruiting pediatric epilepsy studies returned for Canada? Show up to two with study links and contacts, or clearly explain if the search found none. Do not substitute completed studies.

response.answer:
One recruiting pediatric study was returned for Canada:

- **Real World Evidence on the Use of Medical Cannabis in Pediatrics (CAN-RWE)**
  - **NCT:** NCT05863910
  - **Status:** **RECRUITING**
  - **Study type:** Observational
  - **Source population:** Children aged 3–17 years; the registry summary describes children with authorizations for medical cannabis across Canada.
  - **Location:** U Manitoba, Winnipeg, Manitoba, Canada
  - **Epilepsy relevance:** “Epilepsy” is listed as a condition, and eligibility includes medical cannabis authorized for seizures. The registry labels the topic match **indirect_or_unverified** and does not confirm clinical suitability for an individual.
  - **Study link:** [S2](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05863910)
  - **Contact:** Lauren E. Kelly, PhD — lauren.kelly@umanitoba.ca — 2042723149

The registry reported the site as recruiting, but the study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This search returned one listed study; it did not substitute completed studies. It was a bounded search using literal topic terms, so it does not establish that no other studies exist. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/api/v2/studies?query.term=pediatric+epilepsy+AND+%28child+OR+infant%29&filter.overallStatus=RECRUITING&pageSize=20&format=json&query.locn=Canada)

Application limits:
The study team must confirm eligibility and current site availability. This lookup does not determine eligibility or recommend participation.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

**Title:** “FDA requires Boxed Warning about serious mental health side effects for asthma and allergy drug montelukast (Singulair); advises restricting use for allergic rhinitis”

request.question: Where is the official FDA page a parent can use to report a possible medication problem? Does a report by itself show that the medicine caused the problem? Please don't ask me for identifying information or file anything.

response.answer:
The official FDA page is **FDA MedWatch: report a suspected medicine problem**: [S3](https://www.fda.gov/safety/medwatch-fda-safety-information-and-adverse-event-reporting-program)

A report by itself **does not establish that the medicine caused the problem**. The retrieved resource describes it as a suspected problem report and states that reporting does not establish causation. No report was filed, and no identifying information was requested.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

request.question: Find a PubMed paper about levetiracetam while breastfeeding, retrieve its abstract, and summarize only the study design, population and findings actually available. Distinguish drug exposure from infant outcomes.

response.answer:
**“Levetiracetam in lactation: How much is excreted into human breast milk?”** (*British Journal of Clinical Pharmacology*, 2022; PMID 34131926). [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Study design:** The abstract does not state a specific design label. Women with epilepsy treated with levetiracetam completed a questionnaire; researchers measured levetiracetam in serial breast-milk samples from before dosing through 12 hours afterward and in one pre-dose maternal serum sample. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Population:** 20 breastfeeding women and 21 infants, including one set of twins; 16 infants were fully breastfed and five were partially breastfed. The source population is lactation and infant; age, prematurity, and gestational stage are not specified in the retrieved abstract. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Measured drug exposure:** The mean trough breast-milk/maternal-serum ratio was 0.98 ± 0.20. The abstract also reports infant exposure estimates and relative infant exposure values for fully and partially breastfed infants. These are study exposure findings, not dosing advice. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

**Observed infant outcomes:** Three women reported somnolence in their fully breastfed infants; the abstract states that this resolved shortly after switching to partial breastfeeding. It also states that all infants gained weight according to age. The abstract’s suggestion that somnolence could be related to breast-milk exposure is the authors’ interpretation, not proof of causation. [S5](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/34131926/)

The abstract was retrieved successfully for this paper; no requested record was unreturned or missing abstract text. The lookup covered this requested PubMed record only, not a complete literature review.

request.question: What can infant adverse-event reports involving acetaminophen tell a researcher, and what can they not establish about how often side effects occur or whether the medicine caused them? Use the MCP and state the age scope actually queried.

response.answer:
**Age scope queried:** infant reports with age coded in **months 0–12**; records using other age units were excluded. This is only the queried report subset, not all infants. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

### What the reports can show

They provide counts of reported terms within that subset, including:

- Off-label use: **135**
- Drug-administration error: **121**
- Vomiting: **117**
- Pyrexia: **98**
- Product-use issue: **83**
- Overdose: **77**
- Drug ineffective: **65**
- Rash: **60**
- Toxicity to various agents: **58**
- Incorrect dose administered: **56**

These are spontaneous-report terms and reporting volumes; they are not established clinical outcomes. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

### What they cannot establish

- **How often side effects occur:** exposure denominators were unavailable, so the counts cannot establish incidence or risk.
- **Whether acetaminophen caused an event:** spontaneous reports do not establish causation.
- **Risk for all infants or all exposed infants:** the results cannot be generalized to either group.
- **That unlisted events did not occur:** the returned extract does not establish absence of other events.

The MCP also reports that the source population and confirmed age band were not established within the individual reaction records. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22acetaminophen%22+AND+patient.patientonsetageunit%3A802+AND+patient.patientonsetage%3A%5B0+TO+12%5D&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=10)

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

Milk concentrations were higher in hindmilk than foremilk. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- In a case involving a preterm infant, breast-milk concentrations at random times averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. Therefore, infant-level information is missing from the returned exposure extract; no infant specimen type should be inferred. The LactMed summary states that sertraline is usually not detected in infant serum and that norsertraline is often detectable at low levels in infant serum. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\nLactMed reports:\\n\\n- One 4-month-old infant had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and transient agitation. [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9108810/)\\n- In a study of 26 infants, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- In 14 mother\u2013infant pairs, infant whole-blood serotonin values were similar before and after maternal treatment; no adverse effects were reported in those infants. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)\\n- In a follow-up of 25 infants, reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)\\n- No clinical adverse reactions were noted in six infants aged 5\u201334 weeks in one study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)\\n- One case report involving a preterm infant described hyperthermia, altered muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and stated that the symptoms dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued. The case authors attributed the reaction to sertraline exposure through breast milk. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- A small study reported blunted pain responses in infants exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy, with or without breastfeeding exposure; four of the 30 infants had sertraline exposure. The returned LactMed text states that the study lacked a control group of depressed, unmedicated mothers, so the contribution of maternal depression could not be ruled out. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)\\n\\nThe LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the returned extract. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\nThe label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk. It reports a pooled analysis of **53 mother\u2013infant pairs** in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to **2%** of maternal serum levels, with a range of **0\u201315%**; no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. request.question: Using the parent medication information tool, summarize the sertraline evidence from LactMed and the product label. Separate measured milk exposure from observed infant outcomes. Include links and questions to ask a clinician. Do not give dosing or medication decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during breastfeeding

The tool confirmed the ingredient as **sertraline**. The retrieved evidence does not determine an individual treatment plan.

### Measured exposure

LactMed reports the following **milk concentrations**:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers, breast-milk sertraline averaged **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**). [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)
- In a study of 26 women with extensive 24-hour sampling, sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**), and norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). Milk concentrations were higher in hindmilk than foremilk. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In a case involving a preterm infant, breast-milk concentrations at random times averaged **201 mcg/L** for sertraline and **358 mcg/L** for norsertraline. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)

The returned LactMed extract did **not** provide an infant-level concentration excerpt. Therefore, infant-level information is missing from the returned exposure extract; no infant specimen type should be inferred. The LactMed summary states that sertraline is usually not detected in infant serum and that norsertraline is often detectable at low levels in infant serum. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

LactMed reports:

- One 4-month-old infant had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and transient agitation. [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9108810/)
- In a study of 26 infants, no acute adverse reactions were detected during the study. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In 14 mother–infant pairs, infant whole-blood serotonin values were similar before and after maternal treatment; no adverse effects were reported in those infants. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- In a follow-up of 25 infants, reported six-month weight gain was within national growth standards, and mothers reported no abnormal infant effects. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- No clinical adverse reactions were noted in six infants aged 5–34 weeks in one study. [S16](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15367050/)
- One case report involving a preterm infant described hyperthermia, altered muscle-tone regulation, and high-pitched crying. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite and stated that the symptoms dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued. The case authors attributed the reaction to sertraline exposure through breast milk. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- A small study reported blunted pain responses in infants exposed to an SSRI during pregnancy, with or without breastfeeding exposure; four of the 30 infants had sertraline exposure. The returned LactMed text states that the study lacked a control group of depressed, unmedicated mothers, so the contribution of maternal depression could not be ruled out. [S18](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)

The LactMed **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated in the returned extract. The extract does not establish a complete study count or complete outcome record.

### Product-label evidence

The selected DailyMed product was **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, effective date **November 5, 2026**. The exact product and formulation should be confirmed because the retrieved label was not confirmed as the user’s product. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk. It reports a pooled analysis of **53 mother–infant pairs** in which exclusively human-milk-fed infants had average sertraline serum levels equal to **2%** of maternal serum levels, with a range of **0–15%**; no adverse reactions were observed in those infants. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

The label’s lactation section states that there are no data on effects on milk production. The retrieved label also contains adult medicine-taker adverse-reaction information; those findings are not automatically infant outcomes. Sections for warnings, warnings and precautions, boxed warning, and drug interactions were missing from the retrieved label extract, and their absence from this extract is not proof that they are absent from the full label. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Questions to ask a clinician or pharmacist

- Does the selected label match my exact product and formulation?
- How closely do these studies match the infant’s age, prematurity status, health, and feeding pattern?
- Which findings are measured exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
- What uncertainties remain because the returned LactMed sections were truncated?
- What symptoms or changes in feeding, alertness, growth, or behavior should be discussed with a clinician?
- How should the condition being treated and the consequences of changing treatment be considered together?

The MCP’s continuity-of-care notice states: **Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.**

Application limits:
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.

Do not provide medication decisions or doses.\"}", "response_preview": "{\"answer\": \"## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation\\n\\n**Identity:** The evidence brief matched the ingredient **sertraline** exactly. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)\\n\\n### Effects on the lactating person\\n\\n- LactMed reports six patients who observed decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; administered regimens were not reported. It also describes a small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitor exposure in which lactogenesis II was delayed by an average of 16.7 hours, while feeding difficulties after day 4 did not differ statistically between groups. The study included one sertraline-exposed participant, so the finding was not specific to sertraline. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The selected DailyMed product label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk, and that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. This label applies to one selected product, **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)\\n\\n### Measured exposure\\n\\nRetrieved LactMed milk concentrations included:\\n\\n- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7\u2013207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In a 26-woman milk-sampling study: sertraline average **129 mcg/L**, range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**; norsertraline average **258 mcg/L**, range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- Other reported sertraline milk concentrations included **26.4 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **58 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, **<5 mcg/L** in one sample, **11.1\u201324.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6\u201335.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12\u2013288 mcg/L**. Sampling times varied; one passage states that some values might be inaccurate because of sample timing. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n\\nThe returned LactMed concentration extract did not include a complete infant-level measurement section. Separately, the abstract for one study states that detectable concentrations were found in three nursing infants for sertraline and six for desmethylsertraline, with infant serum concentrations below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. The source\u2019s specimen terminology is \u201cinfant serum.\u201d [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)\\n\\nThese are research measurements, not individualized exposure estimates or treatment instructions.\\n\\n### Observed infant outcomes\\n\\n- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one 4-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In several small groups described by LactMed, the source reports no observed acute adverse reactions, no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of study, or no adverse effects in the specific groups studied. These observations were from small, differing populations and do not establish the absence of effects in all breastfed infants. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- A separate abstract involving 12 mothers states that no adverse effects of exposure were observed in the infants studied. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)\\n- LactMed describes one preterm infant born at 33 weeks who developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The case report states that infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite were measured and that symptoms dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued; this is a single case report and the returned extract does not establish how often such an event occurs. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)\\n- A study of infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally alone or prenatally and through breastmilk reported blunted pain responses compared with controls; four of 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. The returned passage states that no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers was included, and the relevant contribution of maternal depression was therefore not established in that study. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)\\n\\n### Report-only context: FAERS\\n\\nFor the query covering reports matching generic name \u201csertraline,\u201d with cohort scope **any**, the returned terms and counts were:\\n\\n| Reported term | Reports |\\n|---|---:|\\n| Nausea | 14,075 |\\n| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |\\n| Fatigue | 13,021 |\\n| Headache | 11,284 |\\n| Anxiety | 10,530 |\\n| Diarrhoea | 10,499 |\\n| Dizziness | 9,741 |\\n| Depression | 9,612 |\\n\\nThe queried population was not established as lactating or infant-specific. These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query does not establish causation, and no exposure denominator was available. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)\\n\\n### Missing-evidence limitations\\n\\n- LactMed\u2019s returned **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The LactMed extract did not establish a study count; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- The PubMed search returned five requested records. Abstract text was retrieved for three; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. No PMIDs were reported as unreturned or as failed abstract lookups. ## Evidence brief: sertraline during lactation

**Identity:** The evidence brief matched the ingredient **sertraline** exactly. [S53](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/36437/properties.json)

### Effects on the lactating person

- LactMed reports six patients who observed decreased milk supply after starting sertraline; administered regimens were not reported. It also describes a small prospective study of serotonin-reuptake inhibitor exposure in which lactogenesis II was delayed by an average of 16.7 hours, while feeding difficulties after day 4 did not differ statistically between groups. The study included one sertraline-exposed participant, so the finding was not specific to sertraline. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The selected DailyMed product label states that published data demonstrate low levels of sertraline and its metabolites in human milk, and that data on effects on milk production are unavailable. This label applies to one selected product, **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**, not all formulations. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured exposure

Retrieved LactMed milk concentrations included:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a 26-woman milk-sampling study: sertraline average **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; norsertraline average **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Other reported sertraline milk concentrations included **26.4 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **58 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, **<5 mcg/L** in one sample, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12–288 mcg/L**. Sampling times varied; one passage states that some values might be inaccurate because of sample timing. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned LactMed concentration extract did not include a complete infant-level measurement section. Separately, the abstract for one study states that detectable concentrations were found in three nursing infants for sertraline and six for desmethylsertraline, with infant serum concentrations below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. The source’s specimen terminology is “infant serum.” [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

These are research measurements, not individualized exposure estimates or treatment instructions.

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one 4-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In several small groups described by LactMed, the source reports no observed acute adverse reactions, no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of study, or no adverse effects in the specific groups studied. These observations were from small, differing populations and do not establish the absence of effects in all breastfed infants. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A separate abstract involving 12 mothers states that no adverse effects of exposure were observed in the infants studied. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- LactMed describes one preterm infant born at 33 weeks who developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The case report states that infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite were measured and that symptoms dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued; this is a single case report and the returned extract does not establish how often such an event occurs. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- A study of infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally alone or prenatally and through breastmilk reported blunted pain responses compared with controls; four of 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. The returned passage states that no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers was included, and the relevant contribution of maternal depression was therefore not established in that study. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)

### Report-only context: FAERS

For the query covering reports matching generic name “sertraline,” with cohort scope **any**, the returned terms and counts were:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhoea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

The queried population was not established as lactating or infant-specific. These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query does not establish causation, and no exposure denominator was available. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Missing-evidence limitations

- LactMed’s returned **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The LactMed extract did not establish a study count; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The PubMed search returned five requested records. Abstract text was retrieved for three; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. No PMIDs were reported as unreturned or as failed abstract lookups. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that research does not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The PubMed search was a bounded relevance search, not a systematic review. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The selected DailyMed label is one product label; the pregnancy section was truncated, and several expected adult warning sections were missing from the returned extraction. Missing sections do not establish absence of information elsewhere in the label. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- Source populations, infant ages, prematurity, breastfeeding extent, co-exposures, and maternal clinical context varied or were unspecified across the retrieved material. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact medicine, formulation, and all active ingredients?
2. How closely do the study populations match my lactation context, including my infant’s age and prematurity history?
3. Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?

[S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Measured exposure

Retrieved LactMed milk concentrations included:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L**, range **7–207 mcg/L**, in a pooled analysis of 15 mothers. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In a 26-woman milk-sampling study: sertraline average **129 mcg/L**, range **11–938 mcg/L**; norsertraline average **258 mcg/L**, range **20–1,498 mcg/L**. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Other reported sertraline milk concentrations included **26.4 mcg/L**, **29 mcg/L**, **58 mcg/L**, **26 mcg/L** in foremilk and **46 mcg/L** in hindmilk, **<5 mcg/L** in one sample, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** with a range of **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**, and **87 mcg/L** with a range of **12–288 mcg/L**. Sampling times varied; one passage states that some values might be inaccurate because of sample timing. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The returned LactMed concentration extract did not include a complete infant-level measurement section. Separately, the abstract for one study states that detectable concentrations were found in three nursing infants for sertraline and six for desmethylsertraline, with infant serum concentrations below the detection limit of most commercial laboratories. The source’s specimen terminology is “infant serum.” [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

These are research measurements, not individualized exposure estimates or treatment instructions.

### Observed infant outcomes

- LactMed reports benign neonatal sleep myoclonus in one 4-month-old infant and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In several small groups described by LactMed, the source reports no observed acute adverse reactions, no clinically noted adverse reactions at the time of study, or no adverse effects in the specific groups studied. These observations were from small, differing populations and do not establish the absence of effects in all breastfed infants. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- A separate abstract involving 12 mothers states that no adverse effects of exposure were observed in the infants studied. [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)
- LactMed describes one preterm infant born at 33 weeks who developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying. The case report states that infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite were measured and that symptoms dissipated after breastfeeding was discontinued; this is a single case report and the returned extract does not establish how often such an event occurs. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S30](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- A study of infants exposed to an SSRI prenatally alone or prenatally and through breastmilk reported blunted pain responses compared with controls; four of 30 infants were exposed to sertraline. The returned passage states that no control group of depressed, nonmedicated mothers was included, and the relevant contribution of maternal depression was therefore not established in that study. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15687451/)

### Report-only context: FAERS

For the query covering reports matching generic name “sertraline,” with cohort scope **any**, the returned terms and counts were:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Nausea | 14,075 |
| Drug ineffective | 13,855 |
| Fatigue | 13,021 |
| Headache | 11,284 |
| Anxiety | 10,530 |
| Diarrhoea | 10,499 |
| Dizziness | 9,741 |
| Depression | 9,612 |

The queried population was not established as lactating or infant-specific. These counts are reporting volume, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes; the query does not establish causation, and no exposure denominator was available. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to sertraline. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22sertraline%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Missing-evidence limitations

- LactMed’s returned **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated, so the extract is incomplete. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The LactMed extract did not establish a study count; reference counts are not study counts. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The PubMed search returned five requested records. Abstract text was retrieved for three; no abstract text was returned for PMID **38133585** or **32320387**. No PMIDs were reported as unreturned or as failed abstract lookups. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that research does not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The PubMed search was a bounded relevance search, not a systematic review. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- The selected DailyMed label is one product label; the pregnancy section was truncated, and several expected adult warning sections were missing from the returned extraction. Missing sections do not establish absence of information elsewhere in the label. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)
- Source populations, infant ages, prematurity, breastfeeding extent, co-exposures, and maternal clinical context varied or were unspecified across the retrieved material. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

### Questions to ask your clinician or pharmacist

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact medicine, formulation, and all active ingredients?
2. How closely do the study populations match my lactation context, including my infant’s age and prematurity history?
3. Which findings measure milk or infant exposure, and which are observed clinical outcomes?
4. Which details are missing from the studies most relevant to my situation?
5. What benefits, risks, and follow-up considerations should we discuss together?
6. What are the risks associated with changing treatment, and how should any change be discussed with the prescribing clinician?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. This brief cannot determine an individualized medication plan.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.

request.question: Please prepare questions for my clinician about the evidence for sertraline during breastfeeding. Use the evidence brief tool.

response.answer:
## Questions to ask your clinician

The evidence brief suggests asking:

1. Does this evidence apply to my exact sertraline product, formulation, and any other medicines or supplements I use?
2. How closely do the study populations match my situation and my infant’s situation, including infant age, prematurity, health conditions, and degree of breastfeeding?
3. Which findings measure drug exposure, and which report observed maternal, milk-production, or infant outcomes?
4. What is known about sertraline and norsertraline measured in breast milk and in infant specimens?
5. Which findings come from small studies or case reports, and which come from larger studies?
6. How should the reported breastfeeding and milk-supply findings be interpreted when some studies involved antidepressants or SSRIs generally rather than sertraline specifically?
7. What evidence is missing for premature infants, newborns, or longer-term development?
8. What follow-up would you recommend for my infant in my circumstances?
9. How should my clinical need for sertraline and the risks of changing treatment be considered alongside the breastfeeding evidence?
10. Would input from a pharmacist, pediatric clinician, or lactation specialist be useful?

### Measured exposure reported by LactMed

LactMed reported breast-milk concentrations in different study contexts, including:

- Sertraline: **45 mcg/L** (range **7–207 mcg/L**) in a pooled analysis.
- In a study with repeated sampling: sertraline **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and norsertraline **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**).
- At two months postpartum in one report: sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L**.
- In one preterm-infant case, breast-milk sertraline and norsertraline averaged **201 mcg/L** and **358 mcg/L**, respectively, at random sampling times.
- Foremilk and hindmilk concentrations collected 13 hours after administration were **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively.
- Other reported milk measurements included **less than 5 mcg/L**, **11.1–24.5 mcg/L**, **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**), and **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**).

The returned LactMed extract did **not** include a complete infant-level concentration section; infant-level information was retrieved separately in the PubMed abstract for one study, which stated that sertraline was detected in three nursing infants and desmethylsertraline in six. These are research measurements, not individualized dosing guidance. [S56](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/) [S52](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9286185/)

### Retrieval limitations

The evidence brief was partial: LactMed’s **Drug Levels** and **Effects in Breastfed Infants** sections were truncated. PubMed abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested records; no abstract text was returned for PMIDs **38133585** and **32320387**. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that the research does not exist. [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22sertraline%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22sertraline%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Lactation%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Breast+Feeding%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Milk%2C+Human%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+lactat%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfeed%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+breastfed%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json) [S47](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38133585/) [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32320387/)

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. The retrieved evidence cannot determine an individual benefit–risk balance.

Application limits:
These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.
Human clinical framing review remains required. This generated answer is not clinically validated.
Stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks. Discuss changes with the prescribing clinician. This tool cannot advise starting, stopping, or changing treatment.
PubMed abstract coverage: abstract text was retrieved for 3 of 5 requested PMIDs. No abstract text was returned for PMID(s): 38133585, 32320387. Missing abstract text is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that a study or research does not exist. Titles alone are not outcome evidence.
Structured evidence rows (retrieval inventory)
| Evidence axis | Extracted findings | Context-only passages | Gap statements |
|---|---|---:|---:|
| Effect on the pregnant or lactating person | 19 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 0 |
| Measured transfer or exposure to fetus or infant | 31 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 0 |
| Observed outcomes in fetus or infant | 24 extracted candidate passages; source interpretation requires review. | 0 | 2 |
These are counts of extracted passages, not studies or proven effects. Context-only passages and gap statements are counted separately. Empty rows do not establish absence of evidence elsewhere or safety. This inventory does not replace the cited findings or validate applicability.

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

## Pregnancy evidence brief: daridorexant

**Identity:** Daridorexant was exactly matched to the ingredient daridorexant. [S15](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/2591497/properties.json)

### Effects on the pregnant person

**Empty row — no observed maternal pregnancy-effect findings were retrieved.**

The product label states that no human pregnancy data are available to evaluate risks of major birth defects, miscarriage, or other adverse maternal or fetal outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef)

### Measured fetal or infant exposure

**Empty row — no measured human fetal exposure, placental-transfer measurement, or infant-level concentration was retrieved.**

### Observed fetal or infant outcomes

**Empty row — no observed human fetal or infant outcome findings were retrieved.**

**Animal evidence, separate from human pregnancy evidence:** The label reports that animal reproduction studies did not show fetal toxicity or malformation in rats or rabbits in the described studies. It also reports no maternal or developmental toxicity in a rat gestation-and-lactation study. These are animal observations, not human pregnancy outcomes. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef)

### FAERS report-only context

The returned FAERS query matched reports containing these terms:

| Report term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| FOETAL EXPOSURE DURING PREGNANCY | 11 |
| PREMATURE BABY | 10 |
| HYPOTONIA NEONATAL | 9 |
| MOANING | 9 |
| NEONATAL BEHAVIOURAL SYNDROME | 9 |
| NEONATAL RESPIRATORY DISTRESS | 9 |
| CARDIAC DISORDER | 7 |
| CARDIOMEGALY | 7 |

These are reporting volumes from the queried subset, not confirmed clinical outcomes, incidence rates, or evidence of causation. The source population was not established, and exposure denominators were unavailable; the results cannot be generalized to all infants or all exposed people. [S1](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22daridorexant%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S11](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

### Maternal pharmacokinetic data retrieved

**No maternal pharmacokinetic data were retrieved** from the label’s Clinical Considerations section or the bounded PubMed search. The pharmacokinetic query returned no records; this means no records were returned by that query, not that evidence is absent elsewhere or that the medicine is safe. [S7](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=3a2d1503-b816-40c9-9fac-7e03c5a3bcef) [S9](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22daridorexant%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22daridorexant%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29+AND+%28%22Pharmacokinetics%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22Drug+Elimination+Routes%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pharmacokinetic%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+clearance%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22area+under+the+curve%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+%22dose+adjustment%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=3&sort=relevance&retmode=json)

- Phone: **1-833-400-9611**
- Status as listed: **Ongoing**

This lookup does not recommend participation or determine eligibility. # Pregnancy evidence brief: lamotrigine

**Identity:** Lamotrigine was matched exactly in RxNorm (RxCUI 28439). [S26](https://rxnav.nlm.nih.gov/REST/rxcui/28439/properties.json)

**Evidence status:** Evidence was retrieved, but this is a bounded source review rather than a systematic review or clinical validation. The retrieved evidence does not determine an individual treatment plan.

## 1. Effects on the pregnant person

### Lamotrigine-specific maternal effects

**No lamotrigine-specific maternal adverse-outcome findings were retrieved in the reviewed pregnancy material.** This is not evidence that maternal effects are absent. The selected DailyMed label’s standalone adult adverse-reaction and warning sections were missing from the retrieval, so those sections cannot be assessed here. The selected product was:

- **LAMOTRIGINE KIT (LAMOTRIGINE) KIT LAMOTRIGINE TABLET [OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.]**
- SPL version 15
- Effective date: October 12, 2026

DailyMed states that this is one selected product label rather than all lamotrigine formulations, and that its in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Underlying-condition context

For pregnancy in people with epilepsy, the label describes disease-associated maternal and embryofetal risks, including obstetric complications and risks associated with untreated or poorly controlled convulsive seizures. These are not lamotrigine-specific adverse effects. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

A pregnancy-and-lactation review states that antiseizure treatment may be required to protect pregnant people with epilepsy from seizures; its abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific maternal outcome estimate. [S23](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/37684052/)

## 2. Maternal pharmacokinetic evidence

### Clinical Considerations

The label states that physiological changes during pregnancy may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect. It reports decreased lamotrigine concentrations during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. The label frames possible treatment adjustment as a clinician consideration; it does not provide an individualized plan. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Literature

- A pregnancy review states that physiological changes during pregnancy affect antiseizure-medication levels and seizure risk, and discusses serum-concentration monitoring. The abstract does not provide a lamotrigine-specific quantitative PK result. [S19](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/32768086/)
- A review of lamotrigine and other antiseizure medicines in pregnancy and breastfeeding explicitly covers clinical pharmacokinetics, but the retrieved abstract provides only the review scope; detailed lamotrigine PK findings were not retrieved. [S20](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/33573557/)
- A naturalistic study of **60 mothers** measured psychopharmacologic medication concentrations in serum and breastmilk at different time points and followed exposed children during the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high concentration-by-dose ratio in breastmilk for lamotrigine, but it does not provide a verified numeric maternal pregnancy concentration or lamotrigine-specific pregnancy PK trajectory. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

**PK gap:** No verified numeric lamotrigine maternal clearance, concentration, exposure, or area-under-the-curve result was retrieved in the reviewed passages. The MCP-generated interpretation is that the available PK passages require inspection of the underlying study population and design; no personalized dose adjustment was inferred.

## 3. Fetal exposure

No quantitative fetal lamotrigine concentration or fetal-to-maternal concentration ratio was retrieved.

The retrieved pregnancy label reports fetal outcomes among exposed pregnancies but does not provide measured fetal concentrations. A currently listed recruiting study concerns antiseizure-medication clearance, maternal blood concentrations, and exposure to unborn children and nursing infants; its registration and planned measurements are not observed outcome findings. [S8](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05450978)

The retrieved breastmilk concentration statement from the 60-mother study concerns lactation exposure, not fetal exposure, and should not be used as a fetal concentration estimate. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

## 4. Observed fetal and infant outcomes

### Human pregnancy-registry findings reported in the label

For **lamotrigine monotherapy during the first trimester**, the label reports:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2%** of **1,558** exposed infants; reported 95% CI **1.6%–3.1%**.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0%** of **1,562** exposed infants.
- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9%** of **2,514** first-trimester exposures; reported 95% CI **2.3%–3.7%**.

The label states that overall malformation frequency was similar to general-population estimates. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label also reports that the NAAED Pregnancy Registry observed isolated oral clefts among **2,200** infants exposed early in pregnancy, with a reported frequency of **3.2 per 1,000** and a reported 95% CI of **1.4–6.3**, described in that registry analysis as threefold higher than unexposed healthy controls. The label states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. It also reports a European case-control study with an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45** and a 95% CI of **0.8–2.63**. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It also states that differences in outcome definitions, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limit the conclusions. Underlying study counts and detailed subgroup results were not provided in the retrieved passage. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Mixed-medication observational findings

A naturalistic study of 60 mothers reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The returned abstract concerns multiple psychotropic medicines and does not establish that these findings were specific to lamotrigine. The source population labels were mixed: pregnancy, lactation, neonate, and child. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

### Guideline abstract

The AAN/AES/SMFM practice-guideline abstract addresses congenital, perinatal, and neurodevelopmental outcomes after antiseizure-medication exposure among children born to people with epilepsy of childbearing potential. The abstract includes lamotrigine among the medicines considered, but it does not provide lamotrigine-specific outcome estimates beyond the label findings summarized above. [S24](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/38748979/)

### Animal findings

The label reports developmental findings in pregnant mice, rats, and rabbits, including fetal body-weight changes, skeletal variations, rat offspring neurobehavioral findings, and decreased fetal folate concentrations. These are animal findings and are not human fetal outcomes. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

## 5. FAERS report-only context

The returned FAERS query covered reports matching generic-name lamotrigine plus the reaction term “foetal exposure during pregnancy”; it was **not a complete exposed population**. Returned report terms and counts were:

| Reported term | Reports |
|---|---:|
| Foetal exposure during pregnancy | 3,527 |
| Atrial septal defect | 357 |
| Congenital anomaly | 327 |
| Premature baby | 257 |
| Ventricular septal defect | 205 |
| Patent ductus arteriosus | 153 |
| Spina bifida | 143 |
| Hypospadias | 135 |

These are spontaneous-reporting volumes, not rates or confirmed clinical outcomes. The returned query did not provide an exposure denominator, did not establish causation, and did not confirm the source population for each term. These results cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to lamotrigine. [S2](https://api.fda.gov/drug/event.json?search=patient.drug.openfda.generic_name%3A%22lamotrigine%22+AND+patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt%3A%22foetal+exposure+during+pregnancy%22&count=patient.reaction.reactionmeddrapt.exact&limit=8) [S13](https://open.fda.gov/apis/drug/event/)

## 6. Evidence gaps and retrieval limits

- The PubMed search returned **690 records**, but the reviewed set was bounded and not a systematic review. [S10](https://eutils.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/entrez/eutils/esearch.fcgi?db=pubmed&term=%28%28%22lamotrigine%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BSubstance+Name%5D+OR+%22lamotrigine%22%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29%29+AND+%28%22Pregnancy%22%5BMeSH+Terms%5D+OR+pregnan%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D+OR+gestation%2A%5BTitle%2FAbstract%5D%29&retmax=5&sort=relevance&retmode=json)
- All **8 requested PubMed records had abstract text retrieved**; none were reported as lacking an abstract, unreturned, or failed in the abstract-coverage field. This does not make the literature search exhaustive.
- No verified numeric fetal lamotrigine concentration was retrieved.
- No verified numeric maternal pregnancy PK result specific to lamotrigine was retrieved.
- Maternal adverse-reaction and adult warning sections were missing for the selected DailyMed label.
- Study populations, gestational timing, co-medications, epilepsy severity, and comparator details were not consistently available in the retrieved abstracts.
- A curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed was not identified in this source review. The MCP identifies this as a coverage limitation, not proof that no other resource exists. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4) [S29](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S30](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

## Questions for a clinician

- Does this evidence apply to the exact lamotrigine formulation and all other medicines involved?
- Which findings apply to lamotrigine monotherapy versus polytherapy?
- How closely do the registry populations match the pregnancy context, including gestational timing and underlying condition?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medicine can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. Human clinical framing review remains required; this generated answer is not clinically validated.

These FAERS results cover only the queried report subset. They cannot be generalized to all infants or all people exposed to the medicine, and cannot establish incidence or causation.

response.answer:
## Count-only coverage for daridorexant in pregnancy

The MCP returned counts only; no narrative findings were retrieved. The counts are not comparable across sources and do not establish evidence quality, clinical safety, or what any study found. Zero matches may reflect query, indexing, snapshot, or population limits. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/)

| Source | Returned count/status | What the count establishes | What it does not establish |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **PubMed** | **3 matches** | Three records matched the returned daridorexant-and-pregnancy query. | The count does not establish verified human outcomes, distinct studies, or evidence quality. The query reported that the daridorexant MeSH phrase was not found. [S4](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/) |
| **ClinicalTrials.gov** | **4 matches** | Four registrations matched `daridorexant AND (pregnancy)`. | The count does not establish posted results, enrollment, outcomes, or confirmed age-band applicability. [S1](https://clinicaltrials.gov/) |
| **DailyMed** | **1 match** | One name-matched product label was returned. | The count does not establish population-specific sections, current FDA approval, or independent evidence. [S2](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/) |
| **LactMed** | **Not applicable; no count** | LactMed was not used for this pregnancy count because it is lactation-only. | It does not provide pregnancy or general pediatric evidence. |
| **MPRINT Gold snapshot** | **0 literal drug-name row matches; 0 distinct PMIDs** | No literal daridorexant match was found in the selected MPRINT Gold snapshot tables. Snapshot date: **November 17, 2026**. | This does not establish that no relevant evidence exists elsewhere. The MCP reports that the lookup used literal drug-name row matching in selected snapshot tables, without name resolution or full portals; rows are not distinct studies. [S3](https://github.com/langli-lab/mprint-kp-data) |

This was a bounded, count-only lookup, not full evidence retrieval. The MCP states that its pregnancy coverage review did not identify a curated federal pregnancy counterpart to LactMed; that is a source-review finding, not proof that no such resource exists. [S6](https://www.fda.gov/drugs/labeling/questions-and-answers-pregnancy-and-lactation-labeling-rule) [S7](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501922/)

Informational only; not medical advice. Compiled from public NIH/NLM/FDA data, which may be incomplete or out of date. Patients should talk to a clinician, pharmacist or poison control before starting, stopping or changing any medication.

[S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)\\n- In a study of 26 women with extensive 24-hour milk sampling: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11\u2013938 mcg/L**) and norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20\u20131,498 mcg/L**). The source states that concentrations were higher in hindmilk than foremilk. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)\\n- In four mothers at two months postpartum: sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L** at random sampling times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)\\n- In one mother, foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after an exposure contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively.
