request.question: Give a balanced research summary of sertraline during lactation, with adverse findings and the relevant source context together. Distinguish observed infant outcomes from milk measurements, describe limits in study size or design, and prepare questions for a clinician. No treatment decisions.

response.answer:
## Sertraline during lactation

### Measured exposure

The retrieved LactMed record reports these **milk concentrations**:

- In a pooled analysis of 15 mothers: sertraline **45 mcg/L** on average, range **7–207 mcg/L**. [S15](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15169695/)
- In a study of 26 women with extensive 24-hour milk sampling: sertraline averaged **129 mcg/L** (range **11–938 mcg/L**) and norsertraline averaged **258 mcg/L** (range **20–1,498 mcg/L**). The source states that concentrations were higher in hindmilk than foremilk. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In four mothers at two months postpartum: sertraline **26.4 mcg/L** and norsertraline **29 mcg/L** at random sampling times. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In one mother, foremilk and hindmilk collected 13 hours after an exposure contained **26 mcg/L** and **46 mcg/L**, respectively. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In nine women providing first-week postpartum trough samples, sertraline was **<5 mcg/L** in one woman and **11.1–24.5 mcg/L** in the other eight; the source notes that timing could affect these values. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In six women providing random samples, the median sertraline concentration was **11.3 mcg/L** (range **3.6–35.7 mcg/L**); the source notes that the sampling timing might make these values inaccurate. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- In 15 mothers whose milk was sampled at prespecified times over two days, the average concentration was **87 mcg/L** (range **12–288 mcg/L**). [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

These are research measurements, not administered amounts or individualized exposure estimates. The retrieved LactMed extract does **not** include a complete infant-level concentration passage: its infant-level information is missing from the returned Drug Levels extract, which was truncated. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Observed infant outcomes

- One **4-month-old infant** had benign neonatal sleep myoclonus and spontaneously resolving agitation in a case report. The retrieved passage does not establish that sertraline caused either finding. [S44](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/9108810/)
- In a study of **26 infants**, no acute adverse reactions attributed to sertraline in milk were detected during the study. [S12](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12590627/)
- In a study of **14 mother–infant pairs**, infant whole-blood serotonin values were measured before and after maternal treatment; the report states that none of the infants experienced adverse effects. [S11](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11578995/)
- In a report involving **25 infants**, the authors reported normal six-month weight gain and no abnormal effects reported by the mothers. [S13](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/12716242/)
- A case report describes a **preterm infant born at 33 weeks** who developed hyperthermia, muscle-tone regulation disorders, and high-pitched crying during the first days after birth while exposed during pregnancy and breastfeeding. The report also described infant serum concentrations of sertraline and its metabolite, genetic findings affecting metabolism, and symptom improvement after breastfeeding was discontinued. Because prenatal exposure, prematurity, and infant metabolism were also present, the contribution of each factor cannot be separated from this retrieved passage. [S26](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/23249132/)
- An uncontrolled survey of **930 mothers** reported infant discontinuation-type symptoms in about 10% of infants exposed to antidepressants, but the result was not sertraline-specific and did not establish causation. [S21](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/20807106/)
- One report described infant sedation when the mother was also taking other medicines; the retrieved evidence does not establish that sertraline alone caused the sedation. [S25](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/22504099/)

### Lactating-person findings and context

LactMed includes a report from six patients who described decreased milk supply after starting sertraline. It also describes a small study of eight mothers taking serotonin-reuptake inhibitors, including one sertraline user, in which onset of milk secretory activation was delayed compared with 423 mothers who were not taking an inhibitor. These findings are not sertraline-specific and do not establish causation. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

The selected DailyMed record states that published lactation data show low levels of sertraline and metabolites in human milk, reports no adverse reactions in a pooled analysis of 53 mother–infant pairs, and states that data on effects on milk production are unavailable in that label. The selected product is **SERTRALINE HYDROCHLORIDE TABLET [REMEDYREPACK INC.]**; the lookup did not confirm that it matches every sertraline product or formulation. The label’s retrieved adverse-reaction section concerns the medicine-taker label population and is not automatically evidence of infant outcomes. Several expected label sections were not returned, including warnings, boxed warning, and drug-interactions sections. [S1](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=687ebdc4-6946-454e-8d46-3207488ccf32)

### Evidence limitations

- The retrieved LactMed Drug Levels and Effects in Breastfed Infants sections are truncated; the record should not be treated as complete. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- The returned evidence includes small studies, case reports, observational reports, an uncontrolled survey, and biomarker measurements; a definitive study count was not established in the retrieved record. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Study details vary in infant age, prematurity, breastfeeding extent, prenatal exposure, co-medications, sampling timing, and follow-up.
- A finding that no adverse outcome was observed in a small study does not establish that adverse outcomes cannot occur.
- The LactMed record was revised August 15, 2026, and the retrieved package was published October 22, 2026; the MCP advises checking the linked record for later updates. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

### Questions for a clinician or pharmacist

1. Does the selected label match the exact sertraline product and formulation?
2. Which evidence concerns milk concentrations, which concerns infant specimens, and which concerns observed infant outcomes?
3. How closely do the studies match the infant’s age, gestational age, prematurity status, health conditions, and feeding pattern?
4. How should the isolated case reports be interpreted when prenatal exposure, prematurity, or other medicines were also present?
5. What information would help distinguish an observed infant symptom from medication exposure or another explanation?
6. Is there evidence in this case concerning milk production or breastfeeding progress?
7. What are the risks associated with changing treatment, and what should be discussed with the prescribing clinician?

The MCP-generated continuity-of-care notice states that stopping or changing a medication can also carry risks and should be discussed with the prescribing clinician. Human clinical framing review remains required; this generated summary is not clinically validated.

- The returned evidence includes small studies, case reports, observational reports, an uncontrolled survey, and biomarker measurements; a definitive study count was not established in the retrieved record. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)
- Study details vary in infant age, prematurity, breastfeeding extent, prenatal exposure, co-medications, sampling timing, and follow-up.
- A finding that no adverse outcome was observed in a small study does not establish that adverse outcomes cannot occur.
- The LactMed record was revised August 15, 2026, and the retrieved package was published October 22, 2026; the MCP advises checking the linked record for later updates. [S47](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/books/NBK501191/)

1. Does the selected label match the exact sertraline product and formulation?

4. How should the isolated case reports be interpreted when prenatal exposure, prematurity, or other medicines were also present?
5. What information would help distinguish an observed infant symptom from medication exposure or another explanation?
6. Is there evidence in this case concerning milk production or breastfeeding progress?

## Lamotrigine pregnancy evidence

**Scope and label context.** The evidence brief identified lamotrigine exactly (RxCUI 28439). It used one selected DailyMed product label—**LAMOTRIGINE KIT, OWP Pharmaceuticals, Inc.**, SPL version 15, effective October 12, 2026—not all formulations. The pregnancy section is truncated in the broader label extract; the returned PLLR pregnancy subsections include the key human-data passages. DailyMed states that its in-use labeling can differ from the latest FDA-approved labeling. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Maternal effects and underlying disease

The pregnancy label states that most lamotrigine pregnancy data come from women with **epilepsy**. It also describes pregnancy-associated risks reported with epilepsy, with or without antiseizure-medication exposure, including preeclampsia, preterm labor, hemorrhage, placental abruption, poor fetal growth, prematurity, fetal death, and maternal mortality. These passages describe underlying-disease and treatment-context risks; they do not establish that lamotrigine caused each outcome. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label reports that physiologic pregnancy changes may affect lamotrigine concentrations and therapeutic effect, including reported decreases during pregnancy and restoration of pre-pregnancy concentrations after delivery. This is label pharmacokinetic context, not an individualized medication plan. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

No maternal lamotrigine adverse-effect outcome was provided in the retrieved pregnancy-specific evidence axes. The selected label’s standalone adult adverse-reaction, warnings, and precautions sections were missing in the extract; this is a retrieval limitation, not evidence that those sections contain no information. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

### Fetal or infant exposure

No quantitative fetal lamotrigine concentration was retrieved.

A mixed psychotropic-medication study of **60 mothers** measured maternal serum and breastmilk at different time points and followed exposed children for the first 12 months. Its abstract reports a high breastmilk concentration-by-dose ratio for lamotrigine, but it does not provide a lamotrigine-specific numeric concentration in the returned text. The study’s population included pregnancy, lactation, neonates, and children, and its findings covered multiple medications rather than lamotrigine alone. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

A recruiting ClinicalTrials.gov study, **NCT05450978**, is investigating antiseizure-medication clearance and exposure to unborn children and nursing infants in pregnant adult women with epilepsy. It has no posted results; the planned investigation is not evidence that an exposure or outcome has been demonstrated. [S8](https://clinicaltrials.gov/study/NCT05450978)

### Observed fetal and infant outcomes

The DailyMed label reports first-trimester **lamotrigine-monotherapy** registry findings:

- International Lamotrigine Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.2% of 1,558 infants**; 95% CI 1.6%–3.1%.
- NAAED Pregnancy Registry: major congenital malformations in **2.0% of 1,562 infants**.
- EURAP: major birth defects in **2.9% of 2,514 exposures**; 95% CI 2.3%–3.7%.

The label states that the frequency of major congenital malformations was similar to general-population estimates. The returned extract does not provide a complete account of underlying disease, co-medications, or all comparator details for each registry. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

For isolated oral clefts, the label reports that the NAAED registry observed **3.2 per 1,000 among 2,200 infants**, described in the label as a threefold increase versus unexposed healthy controls. The label also states that this finding was not observed in other large international pregnancy registries. A European case-control study reported an adjusted odds ratio of **1.45**, with 95% CI 0.8–2.63. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The label states that meta-analyses evaluated fetal death, stillbirth, preterm birth, small-for-gestational-age birth, and neurodevelopmental delay. It further states that the available data did not suggest increased risk with lamotrigine monotherapy, while differences in outcome definition, ascertainment methods, and comparator groups limited the conclusions. [S9](https://dailymed.nlm.nih.gov/dailymed/lookup.cfm?setid=474fb321-575c-4b97-9dbe-080061652ee4)

The mixed psychotropic-medication study reported no significant differences in birth outcomes between in-utero-exposed and nonexposed newborns and no significant differences in development during the first 12 months. The returned abstract does not provide lamotrigine-specific outcome counts, so this finding should not be treated as a lamotrigine-only result. [S22](https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/36103361/)

The label also reports developmental findings in pregnant animals, including reduced fetal body weight, skeletal variations, neurobehavioral abnormalities, offspring mortality, and decreased fetal folate concentrations.
